front: What are the main components of a typical LSM-tree write path?
back: A write-ahead log, a mutable in-memory table, immutable flushed tables, and background compaction.
accepted_answers: A write-ahead log, a mutable in-memory table, immutable flushed tables, and background compaction.
hint: Durability, memory, disk, maintenance.

front: Why does an LSM tree append to a WAL before acknowledging an in-memory write?
back: The memtable is volatile, so the log is needed to reconstruct accepted writes after a crash.
accepted_answers: The memtable is volatile, so the log is needed to reconstruct accepted writes after a crash.
hint: Memory speed needs durable backup.

front: What triggers a memtable flush?
back: Usually a size or time threshold; the active memtable is switched and the old immutable snapshot is written sequentially to disk.
accepted_answers: Usually a size or time threshold; the active memtable is switched and the old immutable snapshot is written sequentially to disk.
hint: A bounded memory component becomes a file.

front: Why must memtable switching be atomic?
back: Every write must belong to either the old flushing table or the new active table, with no lost or duplicated transition window.
accepted_answers: Every write must belong to either the old flushing table or the new active table, with no lost or duplicated transition window.
hint: The write target changes while traffic continues.

front: Why does a flushing memtable remain readable?
back: Until its on-disk replacement is complete and published, it may contain the newest version of keys needed by readers.
accepted_answers: Until its on-disk replacement is complete and published, it may contain the newest version of keys needed by readers.
hint: The new file is not ready yet.

front: What is an SSTable?
back: An immutable sorted on-disk table containing key-value entries.
accepted_answers: An immutable sorted on-disk table containing key-value entries.
hint: A common LSM disk component.

front: Why can an LSM lookup consult several places?
back: The newest value may be in the active memtable, a flushing memtable, or any of several immutable disk tables.
accepted_answers: The newest value may be in the active memtable, a flushing memtable, or any of several immutable disk tables.
hint: Data exists across generations.

front: What role does a Bloom filter play in an LSM tree?
back: It can cheaply prove that a table definitely lacks a key, avoiding unnecessary disk reads, while positive results remain probabilistic.
accepted_answers: It can cheaply prove that a table definitely lacks a key, avoiding unnecessary disk reads, while positive results remain probabilistic.
hint: No false negatives, possible false positives.

front: Why does a Bloom-filter false positive not corrupt correctness?
back: It only causes an unnecessary table lookup; the actual table search still verifies whether the key exists.
accepted_answers: It only causes an unnecessary table lookup; the actual table search still verifies whether the key exists.
hint: It changes cost, not truth.

front: Why are sparse indexes useful for SSTables?
back: Because entries are sorted, the index can point to ranges or blocks rather than storing one pointer per key.
accepted_answers: Because entries are sorted, the index can point to ranges or blocks rather than storing one pointer per key.
hint: Ordering reduces index density requirements.

front: How is an update represented in an immutable LSM component?
back: A newer entry for the same key is appended to a later component; reads choose the newest visible version.
accepted_answers: A newer entry for the same key is appended to a later component; reads choose the newest visible version.
hint: Do not overwrite the old file.

front: How is deletion represented in an LSM tree?
back: A tombstone is written as a newer version so older values are hidden until compaction can safely discard both.
accepted_answers: A tombstone is written as a newer version so older values are hidden until compaction can safely discard both.
hint: Deletion is another record.

front: Why can dropping a tombstone too early resurrect deleted data?
back: An older value may still exist in a lower-level table; removing the tombstone before that value is eliminated makes the old value visible again.
accepted_answers: An older value may still exist in a lower-level table; removing the tombstone before that value is eliminated makes the old value visible again.
hint: The marker must outlive hidden copies.

front: What is compaction?
back: The background process that merges immutable tables, resolves versions and tombstones, and writes new consolidated tables.
accepted_answers: The background process that merges immutable tables, resolves versions and tombstones, and writes new consolidated tables.
hint: Maintenance turns many files into fewer files.

front: Why is compaction required in a multicomponent LSM tree?
back: Without it, table count and read amplification grow continuously and obsolete versions consume space indefinitely.
accepted_answers: Without it, table count and read amplification grow continuously and obsolete versions consume space indefinitely.
hint: Foreground write efficiency creates accumulating debt.

front: What correctness rule applies when publishing compaction output?
back: Old input tables must remain readable until the complete replacement is durable and atomically added to the active table view.
accepted_answers: Old input tables must remain readable until the complete replacement is durable and atomically added to the active table view.
hint: Readers must see old or new, never half-built.

front: Why must two concurrent compactions avoid independently consuming the same input table?
back: They could produce conflicting replacements, discard data incorrectly, or corrupt the table-view transition.
accepted_answers: They could produce conflicting replacements, discard data incorrectly, or corrupt the table-view transition.
hint: Coordinate ownership of maintenance inputs.

front: What is size-tiered compaction optimized for?
back: It groups similarly sized tables, generally favoring write throughput but potentially leaving more overlapping data for reads.
accepted_answers: It groups similarly sized tables, generally favoring write throughput but potentially leaving more overlapping data for reads.
hint: Merge peers by size.

front: What is leveled compaction optimized for?
back: It limits overlap within levels to improve predictable reads and space usage, usually at the cost of more rewriting.
accepted_answers: It limits overlap within levels to improve predictable reads and space usage, usually at the cost of more rewriting.
hint: Better reads, higher write amplification.

front: Why can compaction cause latency spikes?
back: It consumes disk bandwidth, CPU, cache capacity, and I/O queues alongside foreground traffic.
accepted_answers: It consumes disk bandwidth, CPU, cache capacity, and I/O queues alongside foreground traffic.
hint: Background work competes with user work.

front: What is write amplification?
back: The ratio between bytes physically written by the storage stack and bytes written by the application.
accepted_answers: The ratio between bytes physically written by the storage stack and bytes written by the application.
hint: One logical write may be rewritten many times.

front: What is read amplification?
back: The extra components, blocks, or indirections consulted to satisfy one logical read.
accepted_answers: The extra components, blocks, or indirections consulted to satisfy one logical read.
hint: Count the work beyond the requested record.

front: What is space amplification?
back: The additional physical storage used beyond the current logical dataset because of obsolete versions, metadata, and layout overhead.
accepted_answers: The additional physical storage used beyond the current logical dataset because of obsolete versions, metadata, and layout overhead.
hint: Logical size versus actual footprint.

front: How does the RUM trade-off guide storage design?
back: A structure cannot simultaneously minimize read cost, update cost, and memory overhead; improving one dimension usually taxes another.
accepted_answers: A structure cannot simultaneously minimize read cost, update cost, and memory overhead; improving one dimension usually taxes another.
hint: Read, Update, Memory.

front: Why do LSM trees often excel at sustained write-heavy workloads?
back: They transform small random updates into sequential WAL appends, in-memory changes, and batched sequential flushes.
accepted_answers: They transform small random updates into sequential WAL appends, in-memory changes, and batched sequential flushes.
hint: Turn random writes into ordered batches.

front: Why can a B-Tree outperform an LSM tree for latency-sensitive point reads?
back: A B-Tree usually follows one search path, while an LSM read may check several components and wait behind compaction activity.
accepted_answers: A B-Tree usually follows one search path, while an LSM read may check several components and wait behind compaction activity.
hint: Fewer candidate locations.

front: What workload question matters more than asking whether B-Trees or LSM trees are universally better?
back: Ask about read/write ratio, range scans, latency tail, dataset size, storage medium, compaction budget, and operational constraints.
accepted_answers: Ask about read/write ratio, range scans, latency tail, dataset size, storage medium, compaction budget, and operational constraints.
hint: There is no context-free winner.

front: What is Bitcask's basic design idea?
back: Append values to log segments and keep an in-memory hash map from each key to its latest record location.
accepted_answers: Append values to log segments and keep an in-memory hash map from each key to its latest record location.
hint: Hash index in memory, values in append-only files.

front: What limits Bitcask-style designs for very large keyspaces?
back: The complete key-to-location index may need to fit in memory, so index memory grows with key cardinality.
accepted_answers: The complete key-to-location index may need to fit in memory, so index memory grows with key cardinality.
hint: Fast lookup has a RAM cost.

front: What is WiscKey's key-value separation idea?
back: Keep keys and metadata in the LSM tree while storing large values in a separate append-only value log.
accepted_answers: Keep keys and metadata in the LSM tree while storing large values in a separate append-only value log.
hint: Avoid rewriting large values during key compaction.

front: How can key-value separation reduce write amplification?
back: Compaction rewrites small keys and pointers rather than repeatedly copying large values.
accepted_answers: Compaction rewrites small keys and pointers rather than repeatedly copying large values.
hint: Move metadata more often than payload.

front: What cleanup problem does a separate value log create?
back: It needs garbage collection to identify and reclaim value records no longer referenced by the current key index.
accepted_answers: It needs garbage collection to identify and reclaim value records no longer referenced by the current key index.
hint: Old payloads remain after key updates.

front: Why must WAL truncation be coordinated with memtable flush completion?
back: Discarding log records before every accepted write is safely in an on-disk table can make a crash permanently lose data.
accepted_answers: Discarding log records before every accepted write is safely in an on-disk table can make a crash permanently lose data.
hint: The log is the only durable copy during flush.

front: Why can stacking an LSM tree on a log-structured filesystem and SSD be inefficient?
back: Each layer may independently relocate and garbage-collect the same data, multiplying writes, fragmentation, and unpredictable pauses.
accepted_answers: Each layer may independently relocate and garbage-collect the same data, multiplying writes, fragmentation, and unpredictable pauses.
hint: Several append-only layers can amplify one another.

front: What does an SSD flash translation layer do?
back: It maps logical addresses to physical flash pages and manages placement, relocation, erasure, and wear leveling.
accepted_answers: It maps logical addresses to physical flash pages and manages placement, relocation, erasure, and wear leveling.
hint: Flash cannot overwrite pages in place.

front: Why does flash storage erase blocks instead of individual pages matter to databases?
back: Updating a small page can require relocating other live pages and erasing a larger block, increasing write amplification.
accepted_answers: Updating a small page can require relocating other live pages and erasing a larger block, increasing write amplification.
hint: The erase unit is larger than the write unit.

front: Why do sequential append patterns generally fit SSDs better than many tiny random overwrites?
back: They batch writes into fresh pages and reduce read-modify-relocate work in the flash translation layer.
accepted_answers: They batch writes into fresh pages and reduce read-modify-relocate work in the flash translation layer.
hint: Respect flash program/erase behavior.

front: A database's disk usage doubles during compaction. Is that automatically a leak?
back: No. Compaction may temporarily retain old tables while writing replacements; investigate whether space is released after publication and cleanup.
accepted_answers: No. Compaction may temporarily retain old tables while writing replacements; investigate whether space is released after publication and cleanup.
hint: Atomic replacement temporarily needs both generations.

front: A write-heavy service experiences periodic p99 latency spikes although CPU is low. What LSM-specific signal should you inspect?
back: Inspect compaction backlog, flush stalls, disk queue depth, table count, write amplification, and WAL fsync latency.
accepted_answers: Inspect compaction backlog, flush stalls, disk queue depth, table count, write amplification, and WAL fsync latency.
hint: Background storage pressure may be the bottleneck.

back: Scenario-based cards train engineers to recognize operational consequences, not merely recall definitions, which better matches incident and design-review work.
